chunks: What assembly is, versus C and Python. The question: What is assembly? How does it differ from programming languages like C or Python?
A processor only understands machine code, which is binary instruction words. Assembly is the readable text form of those instructions.
It has roughly one line per instruction, so it belongs to one processor family. C is a higher level. You describe what you want, and a compiler turns it into assembly.
Python sits higher still. A separate program called an interpreter reads it and does the work as it goes.
Imagine giving directions to a driver. In Python, you say "take me to the airport", and the driver works out everything.
In C, you give turn-by-turn directions, and a navigator turns them into driving actions. In assembly, you call out each exact steering and pedal move.
Those moves are specific to one car model, just as assembly is specific to one processor family. More control means more work, and you rarely beat a good navigator.
Both paths end at machine code. C is translated ahead of time into assembly, assembled and linked into an image the CPU runs directly.
Python's source becomes bytecode that a native interpreter program executes, so every Python operation costs interpreter work on top of the real instructions.
Machine code: the binary instruction words a processor executes. Assembly: text names for machine instructions, such as add or lw (load a word from memory).
ISA: the set of instructions and registers a processor family supports. Assembly is specific to one ISA. Compiler / assembler: the compiler turns C into assembly.
The assembler turns assembly into machine code. Interpreter: a program that reads another program, such as Python code, and runs it step by step.
Register: a tiny, fast storage slot inside the processor.
One C statement, sum += a[i] , becomes about three RISC-V instructions. First lw t2, 0(a0) loads a[i] into a register. Then add t0, t0, t2 adds it into the sum.
Then addi a0, a0, 4 moves the address on to the next element. Each line is one 32-bit machine word. For example, addi x5, x0, 10 is the word 0x00A00293 . That is the whole idea.
"Assembly is the human-readable form of a processor's machine instructions, roughly one line per instruction, so it's specific to one instruction set like RISC-V, ARM or x86.
C is compiled down to it: one C statement becomes several assembly instructions, and the same C can target many processors.
Python is interpreted, so it's another layer further from the hardware.
I'd use assembly for boot code, interrupt entry, tight optimized loops, and for reading disassembly to debug or check what the compiler generated."
